blocks.prompt: 6. Discuss domain, range, and graph of the function \(f(x) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}\).
blocks.explanation:
\(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}\) is an exponential function \(a^{x}\) with base \(a = \frac{1}{3}\), so \(0 < a < 1\).
We must give its domain and range and describe and sketch the graph.
Plan: the same properties as Question 5, but with \(0 < a < 1\) the function decreases, as in Example 8.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = \frac{1}{3^{x}} = 3^{-x}\), base \(a = \frac{1}{3}\).
To find: domain, range and the graph.
Method: properties of \(a^{x}\) with \(0 < a < 1\) (1.4.2) and a table of values.

Domain
\[\text{Dom } f = \,]-\infty, \infty[\, = \mathbb{R}\]
Why: \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}\) is defined for every real \(x\).

Positivity, continuity and range
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} > 0 \text{ for all } x\]
\[x \to -\infty:\ \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = 3^{-x} \to \infty\]
\[x \to \infty:\ \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = \dfrac{1}{3^{x}} \to 0\]
\[\text{Range } f = \,]0, \infty[\]
Why: a positive base gives positive values; the function is continuous and moves between 0 and \(\infty\), never reaching 0.

Intercepts
\[f(0) = \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{0} = 1\]
\(y\)-intercept \((0, 1)\); no \(x\)-intercept.
Why: any non-zero base to the power 0 is 1, and \(f(x) = 0\) has no solution.

Strictly decreasing (and so one-to-one)
If \(x_{1} < x_{2}\), then
\[\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x_{2}} = \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x_{1}} \cdot \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x_{2}-x_{1}} < \left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x_{1}}\]
Why: \(x_{2} - x_{1} > 0\) and the base is less than 1, so \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x_{2}-x_{1}} < 1\). The graph falls from left to right.

Horizontal asymptote
As \(x \to \infty\), \(f(x) \to 0\), so \(y = 0\) is the horizontal asymptote (on the right side).
Why: the curve comes closer and closer to the \(x\)-axis on the right but never touches it.

Table of values and graph
\(x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2\) give \(f(x) = 9, 3, 1, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{9}\).
Plot and join with a smooth falling curve (figure).
Why: \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = 3^{-x}\), so this graph is the mirror image of \(y = 3^{x}\) (Question 5) in the \(y\)-axis.
Check: the answer key's range \(]0, \infty[\) and its falling graph through \((0, 1)\) agree. Its domain is misprinted (see the correction below).
blocks.final_answer: Dom \(f = \,]-\infty, \infty[\), Range \(f = \,]0, \infty[\). The graph passes through \((0, 1)\), has no \(x\)-intercept, lies above the \(x\)-axis, is strictly decreasing (one-to-one) and has the horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) as \(x \to \infty\).

answer_figure.alt: Graph of f(x) = (1/3) to the power x for x from minus 2 to 6. The curve comes down steeply from the left through (minus 2, 9), (minus 1, 3), (0, 1), (1, 1/3) and (2, 1/9), and approaches the x-axis on the right (asymptote y = 0) without touching it.
answer_figure.caption: Graph of f(x) = (1/3)^x: through (0, 1), decreasing, asymptote y = 0

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints Dom \(f = \,]-\infty, \infty]\), with a closed bracket at \(\infty\). \(\infty\) is not a real number, so it can never be included. The correct domain is \(]-\infty, \infty[\) \(= \mathbb{R}\) (as in Question 5). The range \(]0, \infty[\) is printed correctly.
